facts: Hampstead Heath covers nearly 800 acres of parkland, one of London's largest and wildest open spaces.
Parliament Hill, on the Heath, offers a protected view across the London skyline.
The Heath includes several natural swimming ponds, open to bathers year-round.
The museum sits above the Thames Tunnel, the first tunnel ever built under a navigable river, opened in 1843.
It was engineered by Marc Brunel and his son Isambard Kingdom Brunel.
The tunnel now carries London Overground trains beneath the Thames.
Execution Dock at Wapping was used for over 400 years to hang pirates and mutineers, their bodies left until three tides had washed over them.
Wapping was once at the heart of London's docklands, lined with warehouses.
The area has been substantially regenerated into riverside housing since the 1980s.
Shoreditch has become one of London's leading centres for street art and murals.
The area was home to England's first purpose-built playhouse, The Theatre, in 1576.
Shoreditch transformed from an industrial district into a creative and tech hub from the 1990s onward.

landmark: Warner Bros. Studio Tour (via Watford High Street)
facts: The Warner Bros. Studio Tour, 'The Making of Harry Potter', is based at Leavesden Studios near Watford.
The studios were used to film all eight Harry Potter movies.
Watford High Street serves the town centre, a short distance from the studios.
The timber-framed hunting lodge dates from 1543, built for Henry VIII.
It stands at the southern edge of Epping Forest.
Chingford is the northern terminus of one branch of the London Overground network.
The gallery is housed in the childhood home of designer and writer William Morris.
Walthamstow has one of the longest street markets in Europe, running nearly a mile.
Walthamstow Central is a major interchange with the London Underground.
The Horniman Museum holds an eclectic collection including a famously over-stuffed walrus.
It was founded by tea trader Frederick Horniman and given to the public in 1901.
The museum's gardens offer wide views across south London.
Crystal Palace Park was built to house the relocated Great Exhibition building after 1854.
The park still contains Victorian dinosaur sculptures, among the first ever made.
The Crystal Palace itself burned down in a huge fire in 1936.
Kensal Green was the first of London's 'Magnificent Seven' Victorian cemeteries, opened in 1833.
It is the resting place of numerous notable figures including members of the Royal Family.
The cemetery's grand classical monuments reflect Victorian attitudes to death and memorial.

landmark: Goldsmiths, University of London (New Cross Gate)
facts: Goldsmiths has a strong reputation for art, and several Turner Prize winners studied there.
New Cross Gate is a key interchange on the East London line of the Overground.
The area has a long history as a working-class and student neighbourhood.

landmark: Bethnal Green's WW2 shelter disaster memorial
facts: A crowd crush at Bethnal Green tube shelter in 1943 killed 173 people, the largest single loss of civilian life in Britain in WW2.
A memorial staircase, 'Stairway to Heaven', commemorates the disaster.
Bethnal Green developed as a densely populated working-class district of London's East End.
Whitechapel was the location of the unsolved 1888 Jack the Ripper murders.
The East London Mosque, nearby, is one of the largest mosques in Europe.
Whitechapel has been a gateway neighbourhood for successive waves of immigration to London.
Ridley Road Market has traded in Dalston since the Victorian era, reflecting the area's diverse communities.
Dalston became a noted centre for music and nightlife from the 2000s onward.
The area sits within the London Borough of Hackney.
Hackney Empire opened in 1901 as a grand music hall theatre, designed by Frank Matcham.
Charlie Chaplin performed there early in his career.
Hackney Central is a key interchange on the London Overground network.
Camden Market is one of the most visited markets in London, drawing millions of visitors a year.
The area has long been associated with alternative music and fashion subcultures.
Camden Road station is on the Overground's North London Line.
Alexandra Palace hosted the world's first regular high-definition television broadcasts in 1936.
The building has been rebuilt twice after major fires, most recently in 1980.
It sits on a hill with panoramic views across London.
Clapham Junction is often cited as the busiest railway station in Europe by number of trains passing through.
It sits at the crossing point of several major South London rail routes.
The station's name comes from the district of Clapham, though it actually lies in Battersea.
Shepherd's Bush Empire opened as a music hall in 1903 and remains a leading live music venue.
The nearby Westfield London is one of the largest shopping centres in Europe.
Shepherd's Bush sits close to the BBC's former Television Centre.
Imperial Wharf station opened in 2009 to serve a redeveloped former industrial riverside site.
Chelsea Harbour, nearby, is a marina and residential development on the Thames.
The station sits on the West London Line, part of the Overground network.
Canada Water takes its name from the former Surrey Commercial Docks, which handled Canadian timber imports.
The docks closed in the 1970s and the area has since been redeveloped for housing and leisure.
Canada Water is a major interchange between the Overground and London Underground.
Willesden Junction has been a key railway junction in northwest London since Victorian times.
It connects several London Overground lines at multiple platform levels.
The surrounding area developed largely around the railway's presence from the 1860s.
Clissold Park is built around an 18th-century mansion, Clissold House.
Stoke Newington has long been known for its Nonconformist and radical religious history.
The area retains one of London's largest concentrations of Georgian houses outside central London.

landmark: Seven Sisters & the Ancient trees legend
facts: The area is named after a legendary circle of seven elm trees once planted on Page Green.
Seven Sisters is home to a significant Latin American community, centred on Wards Corner market.
The station is a major interchange in north London.

landmark: Highams Park's lake and Epping Forest edge
facts: Highams Park Lake was originally created as an ornamental feature for a country estate.
The area sits close to the eastern edge of Epping Forest.
Highams Park developed as a suburban area in the late 19th century.
Enfield has held a market since medieval times, still trading in the town centre today.
The area was once home to the Royal Small Arms Factory, which produced the Lee-Enfield rifle.
Enfield Town is the terminus of a short Overground branch.
Walthamstow Wetlands is the largest urban wetland nature reserve in Europe.
It occupies a series of Victorian reservoirs still used for London's water supply.
Blackhorse Road station provides one of the main entrances to the wetlands.
Homerton sits within the London Borough of Hackney, historically a working-class district.
Homerton University Hospital is one of the area's major landmarks.
The station is on the Overground's line towards Chingford.
Hackney Wick has become known for its concentration of artist studios and creative businesses.
The area sits directly beside the former Olympic Park site.
Hackney Wick was historically an industrial area on the River Lea.
London Fields Lido is one of the few heated Olympic-length outdoor pools in London, open year-round.
The surrounding park has been common land since at least the 16th century.
London Fields sits within the London Borough of Hackney.
Brockley and Ladywell Cemeteries together form one of south London's largest Victorian burial grounds.
The area developed rapidly with railway-era terraced housing from the 1870s.
Brockley sits in the London Borough of Lewisham.

landmark: Honor Oak Park & One Tree Hill
facts: One Tree Hill, nearby, is said to be where Elizabeth I once picnicked beneath an oak tree.
The hill offers wide views across south and central London.
Honor Oak Park sits between Forest Hill and Peckham Rye.
Penge grew rapidly after the Crystal Palace relocated nearby in the 1850s.
The area sits at the boundary of several south London boroughs.
Penge West station is on the line towards Crystal Palace and Sydenham.
Anerley developed as a residential suburb following the arrival of the railway in the 1850s.
The name is thought to derive from a Scottish word meaning 'lonely' or 'solitary'.
Anerley sits close to Crystal Palace Park.
Wanstead Park was once the grounds of a grand stately home, Wanstead House, demolished in 1825.
The park retains ornamental lakes and woodland from its landscaped past.
It forms part of the wider Epping Forest estate managed by the City of London.
Leyton sits close to the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, developed for the 2012 Games.
The area has a long association with early English football and cricket clubs.
Leyton Midland Road serves the Overground's Gospel Oak to Barking line.
Gospel Oak takes its name from a tree under which open-air sermons were once preached.
The station sits at the southern edge of Hampstead Heath.
Gospel Oak is on the Overground's orbital line towards Barking.
Barking Riverside is one of London's largest new housing developments, built on former industrial land.
The Overground extension to Barking Riverside opened in 2022.
The area sits on the north bank of the Thames in east London.
Woodgrange Park developed as a planned Victorian residential estate.
The area sits in the London Borough of Newham, close to Forest Gate.
The station connects the Overground's Gospel Oak to Barking line.
Emerson Park developed as a leafy residential suburb in outer east London.
The station is served by a short Overground branch from Romford.
The area sits within the London Borough of Havering.

landmark: Watford's Cassiobury Park (via Watford High Street)
facts: Cassiobury Park was once the grounds of a grand country house, now demolished.
It remains one of the largest and most visited parks in Hertfordshire.
Watford High Street serves the town's traditional shopping centre.
Carpenders Park sits on the edge of Greater London, bordering Hertfordshire.
The area developed as a suburban estate in the interwar years.
The station serves the Overground's Watford branch.
The station serves the boundary between Hampstead and Finchley Road's commercial strip.
Frognal is a quiet residential enclave known for large Victorian and Edwardian houses.
The area is close to several of London's cultural and educational institutions.
West Hampstead has three separate stations, an unusual concentration for a London district.
The area developed as a middle-class suburb in the late 19th century.
West Hampstead has long attracted musicians and recording studios.
Kilburn was historically home to one of London's largest Irish communities.
The high road follows the route of the old Roman Watling Street.
Kilburn sits across the boundary of the boroughs of Brent and Camden.
Crouch Hill sits close to Finsbury Park, one of north London's major green spaces.
The area developed with Victorian terraced housing from the 1880s onward.
Crouch Hill station connects the Overground's Gospel Oak to Barking line.
The area sits close to the Regent's Canal in north London.
Barnsbury retains many well-preserved early Victorian squares and terraces.
The station serves the North London Line of the Overground.
Canonbury Tower, a surviving Tudor structure, is one of the oldest buildings in Islington.
The area is known for its well-preserved Georgian squares.
Canonbury sits between Highbury and Dalston.
South Tottenham sits close to the River Lea and its associated reservoirs and marshes.
The area has a long history as a working-class, industrially linked district.
South Tottenham is a key interchange on the Overground's Gospel Oak to Barking line.
Edmonton Green has a long-running open-air market at the heart of its shopping centre.
The area was historically part of the Lea Valley's market gardening belt supplying London.
Edmonton Green sits on the Overground's line towards Cheshunt.
